And now, back to the present: what does our discussion about a human being possessing, as it were, the power to move the Earth tell us about the nature of the universe in general?

In the first place, the discussion in the lecture demonstrates that the Earth, as well as the Earth itself, has a different relationship with our common world of the "earthly" (as opposed to the "heavenly") and with our world of the "human" (as opposed to the "divine"). In the same way, a man is connected with his body as the center, the point of departure and the point of arrival of the soul's journey through the body. (This is not to be taken as a physical, chemical or biological point of view!) Yet the soul in its movement through the body is independent of the body, which is in essence "passive" and dependent on the soul. What happens in the body is always the result of the soul's movement through the body; hence the body is always the effect of the soul's action. If, in the world of the earthly, I am the center, then I am also in the world of the human. This is true, for example, if you make a journey and come back. In the end you return to yourself. This is also true when I have done something bad. In the end, I must answer for myself. (I can try to get away with it, but if I am unsuccessful, then at the very least, it will affect me at the end of my life.) In the world of the earthly, the world of the human, and the world of the divine, what happens with my soul and my spirit is always at the center. It is the starting point and the end of the journey.

We can also see from this lecture that even in the world of the earthly, a "higher" principle of a different order of things, of a higher world, always acts on and affects the world of the earthly. There are thus two orders of things, two principles that affect the universe, and so there must be two universes, two natures, that are affected. In this respect, there must be two ways of looking at the universe. We must consider it as something that belongs to a higher world and as something that belongs to a lower world, both of which are affected by the same principle (although in different ways) and both of which together create the whole universe.

The last thing I would like to say today about the universe is that in this context, too, we must think of man as an entity that has two worlds: the world of the earthly, the human, and the world of the divine. In the earthly, the human, and the divine, the man has a completely different value than in the world of the heavenly. In the earthly, the human, and the divine, a man is the center of all things, whereas in the heavenly he is, if not an object of contempt, then at least a being of little value. In the latter case, he is an object for purposes of manipulation. The heavenly world is different from the earthly, human, and divine worlds in that in the heavenly, the human, and the divine worlds, a man has the power and the value of a "principle" or "spiritual leader," whereas in the heavenly world, he is merely an "object" of someone else's manipulation. The difference between the heavenly and the earthly, human, and divine worlds is not only that what happens in the heavenly is directed from above, whereas in the earthly, human, and divine it is directed from within the earthly, human, and divine worlds. What also changes is the relationship between the man and the "heavenly" power.

This brings me to my final point, which I will not dwell on today. When I discuss the relationship between the heavenly and the earthly, human, and divine worlds, I must say that in the world of the heavenly, human, and divine, the "heavenly" power does not act as it does in the heavenly world. The heavenly, human, and divine worlds are not only the world of the earthly, human, and divine but also the world of the heavenly. Hence in this world, man has a different role, as we have already said; namely, the role of a principle, a "spiritual leader" and even a "god." This is where I must stop today.

(1) "Divine," "human" and "earthly" worlds: the highest, the lowest and the middle worlds of existence, respectively. In the highest of the three, God created man in His own image and likeness; in the middle world, God created man from dust, and from the dust of the earth; in the lowest world, man, having fallen from grace, became like the other animals.
(2) "World of the heavenly, human, and divine" and "world of the earthly" are not precise translations of "wielka świat and ziemia." The former is the closest to "the universe," which, unfortunately, does not appear in the lectures, and the latter is the closest to "nature," which is also not a precise term. The best translation of the Polish terms used here is a "world of the divine, the human and the earthly." "World" here refers to a totality or an order. Thus a "world of the heavenly, human, and earthly" means "a totality of the heavenly, the human, and the earthly" or "an order of the heavenly, the human and the earthly" and not, as it could be taken to mean, the totality of these three "worlds" taken separately.<|endoftext|>
